paragraphs.source_en: She stood there for quite some time, watching until the master's head had vanished from sight. Still receiving no answer, she took two steps forward from the doorway, tapped the matting with the broom, and said, "It is time you got up." Once more she respectfully awaited the master's reply. By this time the master was already awake; because he was awake, he had beforehand withdrawn, head and body together, into the bedding to guard against his wife's assault, lying there with the absurd little hope that if only he did not put his head out she might let him off. But his wife showed no sign of letting him off. Moreover, when his wife had first called him, her voice had come from the doorway, at least six feet away, so he had felt he might be safe; but now the sound of the broom handle striking was as close as three feet, which could not help startling him. That alone would have been bad enough; the second call of "Surely you ought to be up by now" seemed to him, from inside the bedding, to have doubled in both nearness and volume since the first. He realized this would not do, and had no choice but to answer with a muffled "Mm."

paragraphs.source_en: "We shall see who is talking nonsense!" As she said this, the master's wife planted the broom upright with a thud beside the master's pillow, looking rather imposing. Just then, Hatchan, the child of the rickshaw man behind the house, suddenly burst out crying with a loud wail. Whenever the master became angry, Hatchan was certain to cry; this was something the rickshaw man's wife compelled the child to do. Whenever my master lost his temper, the rickshaw man's wife made Hatchan cry; perhaps the Kaneda household rewarded her with a little pocket money for it, but what a burden it must have been for Hatchan. With such a mother, the child was truly unfortunate, forced to cry without cease from morning till night. If the master were to grasp even a little of what was going on here and restrain his anger somewhat, Hatchan would surely live a little longer. Even if Mr. Kaneda had put the rickshaw man's wife up to it, anyone who does such a foolish thing may be judged more fiercely committed to heavenly justice than Heavenly Justice himself. If they made the child cry only when the master grew angry, the child might still have room to breathe; but whenever Mr. Kaneda hired neighborhood ruffians to come shout about the "old Imado-ware badger," Hatchan too had to join in by crying. At times, before it was even clear whether the master would be angry or not, they assumed he surely would be and took the initiative, so Hatchan had to start crying first. At this rate, it becomes impossible to tell whether the master is Hatchan or Hatchan is the master. It takes no trouble to vex the master: give Hatchan a sharp scolding or two, and it is as good as slapping the master across the face. It is said that in ancient times in the West, when a criminal was to be executed but had fled abroad and could not be captured, they would burn an effigy in place of the real person. It appears that among them there must be a strategist versed in Western lore who taught them this cunning device. Whether the students of Rakuunkan Middle School or Hatchan's mother, both are surely troublesome opponents for the resource-poor master. Besides these, there are many others the master cannot deal with; perhaps everyone in the whole neighborhood is beyond him. But that has nothing to do with the matter at hand, so I shall introduce them to you little by little another time.
